messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM warning
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Replying to this publicly, in case anyone has a similar question. The reason for the problem in this case is that one of the "employer" levels has 0 relationships, which is the smallest attainable value in the sample space and therefore has MLE at -?. For binary ERGMs, this would be detected, but for valued ERGMs, this type of detection doesn't work, because 0 is not the smallest value for nodefactor(..., form="sum") in all possible sample spaces (e.g., signed edges).

Also, because there are 31 distinct employers, I recommend increasing the MCMC.samplesize and/or MCMC.interval.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] gof when missing edges are present - why are models terms treated differently than other GOF components?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] gof when missing edges are present - why are models terms treated differently than other GOF components?
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

Consider the following example :

# create a nw with 10 nodes (1 to 10)

nw <- network.initialize(10,directed=F,loops=F,bipartite = F)

# add few edges (1-2, 1-3)

nw <- network.edgelist(matrix(c(1,2,1,3),ncol = 2,byrow = T),nw)

# declare all links to/from 4 and above are missing

nw[4:10,,add.edges=T]=NA

# fit ergm on nw

e.nw=ergm(nw~edges)

#perfom gof

gof(e.nw, GOF = ~distance+degree+triadcensus+model)


Goodness-of-fit for minimum geodesic distance

       obs min  mean max MC p-value
1   22.50  13 21.79  29       0.88
2   20.44  13 20.55  28       0.98
3    1.85   0  2.39   9       0.98
4    0.03   0  0.09   2       0.16
Inf  0.18   0  0.18   9       0.04


...

Goodness-of-fit for model statistics

        obs        min       mean        max MC p-value
       3.00      13.00      21.79      29.00       0.00


In the output above :
     - in "minimum geodesic distance", column "obs" is the average of 
conditional simulations on imputed networks, columns min-mean-max are 
those of unconditional simulations.
     - in the "model statistics", column "obs" is the actual statistics 
in the original network - without imputations, and column min-mean-max 
are the result of unconditional simulations.

As a consequence, while in the case above the "GOF minimum geodesic 
distance" agrees between observed and simulated,
it is never the case that "obs" model statistics terms compare with 
"min-mean-max" in GOF in my experience.

This is because differences in the computation in case of missing edges:
     * first a set of conditional simulations are obtained: missing 
links are imputed using the fitted ergm model with constraints 
~observed, repeat 100 times and compute
     all stats listed in GOF (here : distance, degree, triadcensus and 
model) on the imputed network.
     The average statistics are copied to "obs.XXX" terms BUT FOR THE 
MODEL TERM where it is really the observed term (without imputation) 
that is conserved.
     * second a set of unconditional simulation are obtained, and 
statistics computed on these.

Is there a reason why model terms are treated differently from other 
statistics ?
For consistency with other statistics, I would suggest that the "model 
statistics" computation
  in gof.formula, line 89

84 if ("model" %in% all.gof.vars) {
85   if (!network.naedgecount(nw) | !unconditional) {
86      obs.model <- summary(object)
87    }
88    else {
89      obs.model <- SimCond$obs.model
90    }

should be changed to

89   obs.model <- SimCond$summary.model[, "mean"]


Thanks for your comments



--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Check for correlation between predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, as with linear and logistic regression, multicollinearity can be a problem. The effects on interpretation are similar, but correlation can also interfere with estimation.

To examine it once you've successfully fit the model, mcmc.diagnostics() will show you which statistics are the most correlated. Before fitting the model, you can look at the variance-covariance matrix of the MPLE estimates (vcov(ergm(nw~model, estimate="MPLE")), which should give a pretty good idea (especially for dyad-independent predictors) as well.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

       Network Modeling for Epidemics

       Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the University of Washington that
       provides an introduction to stochastic network models for infectious disease transmission dynamics,
       with a focus on empirically based modeling of HIV transmission. ?It is a ''hands-on'' course, using
       the EpiModel software package in R (www.epimodel.org). EpiModel provides a unified framework for
       statistically based modeling of dynamic networks from empirical data, and simulation of epidemic
       dynamics on these networks. It has a flexible open-source platform for learning and building
       several types of epidemic models: deterministic compartmental, stochastic individual-based, and
       stochastic network models. Resources include simple models that run in a browser window, built-in
       generic models that provide basic control over population contact patterns, pathogen properties and
       demographics, and templates for user-programmed modules that allow EpiModel to be extended to the
       full range of pathogens, hosts, and disease dynamics for advanced research. ?This course will touch
       on the deterministic and individual-based models, but its primary focus is on the theory, methods
       and application of network models.

       The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with?students working in small
       groups. ?On the final day, students have the?option of developing an EpiModel prototype for their
       own research?projects, with input from the instructors, which includes the lead?EpiModel software
       developer, Dr. Samuel Jenness.

       return for a refresher course. ?The EpiModel?package has been significantly enhanced over the last

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Check for correlation between predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaber,

There will always be correlation between predictors in a network model. 
The terms in the model are counts of edge configurations, so the same 
edges are often involved in more than one term.

However, these terms are computed at the network level, so your observed 
data have a single vector of sufficient statistics, so there's no 
correlation you can calculate there.

The correlation is implicit in the conditional logit equation for each 
tie, as this expresses how each term will change if the tie is toggled. 
So, you could construct the matrix of conditional changestats and test for 
correlation there.

But it's probably easier just to check for correlation in the estimated 
coefficients from the model.  You'll find that in output from an ergm fit 
in the "covar" element.

hth,
Martina
